opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest advantage is the hardware ecosystem. If you want to build a complete embodied system, you need motors, actuators, sensors, batteries, reducers, and the ability to iterate on the mechanical design very quickly. In China, especially around Shenzhen and the Yangtze River Delta, the supply chain is very dense. A team can design a new joint or a new hand, get parts made, and have a prototype within a couple of weeks. In the US, the same loop can take months, and it costs a lot more. For robotics that matters a lot, because you don't get the design right the first time. You build, you test, it breaks, you redesign. The faster you can turn that loop, the faster you learn.

The second advantage is cost. Embodied AI ultimately needs a lot of robots deployed in the real world, both to collect data and to create value. If the cost of a humanoid or a mobile manipulator drops significantly, many more robots can get into labs, factories, and homes. Chinese companies have been very good at pushing costs down through manufacturing scale and engineering optimization, and that's very important for the field as a whole.

Third, there's a strong engineering culture of integration. Many Chinese teams are comfortable doing the full stack: mechanical design, electronics, low-level control, and increasingly the learning-based policies on top. That vertical integration lets them optimize the whole system rather than just one piece.

That said, I don't see it as a zero-sum picture. The US still has very strong advantages in foundation models, in AI research, and in compute infrastructure. The "brain" side, things like world models, large-scale simulation, and generalist policies, is where a lot of the frontier research has been happening. What I find exciting is that embodied AI needs both: a capable body that's affordable and reliable, and a capable brain that can generalize. The field progresses fastest when hardware and models co-evolve. So from my perspective, the strengths are quite complementary, and the open research community, open models, open datasets, and shared simulation tools help everyone move forward, wherever the robots are built.

r001.rationale: The response describes Chinese teams doing the full stack—mechanical design, electronics, low-level control, and learning-based policies—and says vertical integration lets them optimize the whole system, which conveys greater control over integration across model, hardware, and software.

r002.rationale: It says China’s dense hardware supply chain enables rapid prototyping in weeks, while the same iteration loop in the US can take months and cost more.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important advantage is the supply chain and how close it sits to the people building the robots. If you are in Shenzhen or the Yangtze River Delta and you need a new actuator, a harmonic reducer, a custom motor, a sensor board, you can get an iteration back in days, sometimes hours. In the US that same loop often takes weeks, because the component is coming from somewhere else and the engineer who designed it is not in the same building. Embodied AI is not like a pure software product where you can iterate just on the model. The body matters, and the body has to be built, broken, and rebuilt many times. So the speed of the hardware loop becomes the speed of the whole system.

The second advantage is cost, and cost is not just about margin. When a humanoid or a mobile manipulator costs a fraction of what it would elsewhere, you can afford to deploy a fleet of them, and a fleet is how you collect real-world data. In embodied AI the data bottleneck is enormous. We do not have an internet of robot experience the way we have an internet of text. The companies that can put many robots into factories, warehouses, and homes early will have a data flywheel, and lower unit cost directly feeds that flywheel.

Third, there is a very deep manufacturing culture and a lot of application scenarios. China has the factories where these robots will actually work, so the feedback from real customers comes fast and it is very concrete. That forces a kind of system-level thinking. You cannot just have a nice policy in simulation; you need the gripper to survive, the battery to last a shift, the integration with the line to work. Chinese teams tend to be good at that full-stack integration because the ecosystem rewards it.

Now I would also be honest about where the US still leads. The frontier foundation models, the largest training clusters, the simulation infrastructure, and a lot of the fundamental research on learning algorithms still come disproportionately from the US. And the best robotics in the long run will be a marriage of a very capable brain and a very capable, affordable body. So my view is not that one side wins. The interesting question is who can close their own gap faster: whether the Chinese companies can build world-class models on top of their hardware and data advantage, or whether the US companies can solve the hardware and deployment problem. Personally I think the hardware and deployment problem is harder to solve purely with money, because it is about ecosystems and time, and that is why I take the Chinese embodied companies very seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the importance of the robot body and says Chinese teams are good at full-stack integration, but it does not clearly state that building the complete system gives a company greater control over integrating its model with its hardware and software.

r002.rationale: The response describes China’s deep manufacturing base, nearby component suppliers, and factory deployment scenarios, and says these enable faster hardware iteration and customer feedback than in the US.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest advantage is the proximity between the people developing the intelligence and the people building the hardware. With an embodied system, those two things have to evolve together. You test a policy on a robot, discover that the actuator or the sensor placement is limiting you, change the design, and test again. The faster you can run that cycle, the faster you can make progress.

Chinese robotics companies can benefit from a dense manufacturing and component ecosystem. That can make it easier to source parts, work closely with suppliers, and iterate on a complete system at a reasonable cost. And cost really matters here: building one impressive prototype is very different from building a fleet that operates reliably and generates useful experience.

The United States has strengths in AI research and software. But strong AI alone doesn’t automatically give you a useful robot. You need mechanical design, controls, manufacturing, and deployment to work together. I think Chinese companies have a real opportunity in that integration. The question is whether they can turn those advantages into robots that consistently do useful work.

r001.rationale: It says intelligence and hardware must evolve together and describes testing a policy, changing actuator or sensor design, and retesting—communicating control over model–hardware integration.

r002.rationale: It identifies China’s dense manufacturing and component ecosystem as making parts sourcing, supplier collaboration, and system iteration easier, implying capabilities that are harder to achieve in the United States.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest advantage is the proximity between the people developing the robot and the people making its components. An embodied system requires much more than a strong AI model. You have to bring together motors, actuators, sensors, batteries, electronics, and manufacturing, and then make all of those work reliably with the software.

Chinese robotics companies can benefit from a very dense manufacturing ecosystem. If a team needs to change a component, test a different design, or reduce cost, having suppliers and manufacturing partners nearby can make that iteration much faster. And there are many potential applications in manufacturing and logistics where teams can learn from actual deployment.

The United States has strengths in foundational AI research, software, and computing. So I wouldn’t say one side has every advantage. But for building a complete embodied system, the ability to repeatedly connect intelligence with hardware, test it, and manufacture it economically is extremely important. That’s an area where Chinese companies have a strong opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response describes connecting AI with hardware and software and iterating quickly, but does not clearly say that building the complete system gives a company greater control over that integration.

r002.rationale: It identifies China’s dense manufacturing ecosystem as helping teams iterate faster and reduce costs, but does not say this enables capabilities that are difficult to achieve in the United States.
